title: C++ Gotchas and Undefined Behaviour
relevance: Interviewers use UB and gotchas to separate candidates who can ship production C++ from those who only know the happy path.

phases.goal: Establish the standard's three categories of incompletely rigid behaviour and what each allows the compiler to do.

must_hit.point: Undefined behaviour means the standard imposes no requirements: the program may crash, output garbage, or appear to work, and the optimiser may assume UB never happens and delete that code path.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names UB as the red zone with no guaranteed outcome and notes that optimisers may erase UB-containing paths.

must_hit.point: Unspecified behaviour means the standard allows two or more valid outcomes and the compiler need not document which it chooses, such as function-argument evaluation order.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts unspecified with UB and cites argument evaluation order (e.g. f(i++, ++i)) as an example.

must_hit.point: Implementation-defined behaviour varies by compiler or platform, but the implementation must choose one outcome and document it, such as sizeof(int) or whether char is signed.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says the choice must be documented and gives sizeof(int) or char signedness as examples.

probes: What is the difference between undefined, unspecified, and implementation-defined behaviour in C++?

hints.1: The standard splits 'not fully rigidly defined' into three named categories.
hints.2: Think about what the compiler may assume, what it may leave undocumented, and what it must document.
hints.3: UB: no requirements and optimisers may delete paths; unspecified: multiple valid outcomes, no documentation required (e.g. argument order); implementation-defined: must pick and document (e.g. sizeof(int)).

phases.goal: Show that the candidate can instantly spot classic UB and well-defined but counter-intuitive gotchas in code.

must_hit.point: Out-of-bounds array or vector operator[] access, null/dangling dereference, double free, reading an uninitialised primitive, and signed integer overflow are all undefined behaviour.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate lists several of these and correctly labels each as UB, not merely a runtime error.

must_hit.point: Unsigned integer arithmetic wraps with modulo arithmetic, whereas signed overflow is UB and optimisers routinely exploit that to delete bounds checks.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts defined unsigned wraparound with signed overflow as UB exploited by optimisers.

must_hit.point: Data races (concurrent access with at least one write and no synchronisation), strict-aliasing violations via incompatible pointer types, invalid static_cast downcasts, modifying an originally const object through const_cast, and returning a reference or pointer to a local are UB.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate identifies at least a couple of these less-common UB forms with the right reason.

must_hit.point: Gotchas that are often well-defined but surprising include the most vexing parse (Widget w() declares a function), integer division truncation (3 / 2 yields 1.0 when assigned to double), floating-point == unreliability, object slicing on by-value base copies, virtual calls in constructors dispatching to the current class, the static initialisation order fiasco across TUs, and member-initialiser order following declaration order not list order.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names several gotchas and distinguishes them from UB where appropriate.

probes: Walk this snippet and say which lines are undefined behaviour versus merely surprising but defined behaviour.

hints.1: Scan first for lifetime, bounds, and signed overflow before tracing 'normal' logic.
hints.2: Separate the UB catalogue (OOB, null, double free, uninit, signed overflow, races, aliasing, bad downcast, const_cast mutate, local return) from gotchas like most vexing parse and slicing.
hints.3: Call out UB with the standard's 'no requirements' framing, then name a defined gotcha such as Widget w() being a function declaration or 3 / 2 truncating.

phases.goal: Connect language rules to intentional API and design choices that trade safety for performance or clarity.

must_hit.point: vector operator[] skips bounds checks for performance; use at() when you want a guaranteed std::out_of_range on invalid access.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains unchecked [] versus throwing at() and ties it to performance.

must_hit.point: Passing a derived object by value into a base parameter slices off derived members and dynamic type; pass Base& or Base* to preserve polymorphism.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes slicing and the reference/pointer fix.

must_hit.point: If a lambda escapes its scope, capture-by-reference on locals dangles; capture by value or return owning values instead.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts [&] escape bugs with [=]/[local] or returning std::string by value.

probes: Why might a library expose unchecked operator[] and a checked at(), and when would you choose each?

hints.1: Think about what the call site pays for on every access.
hints.2: Contrast performance of no bounds check with a guaranteed exception API.
hints.3: operator[] maximises performance without checks; at() throws std::out_of_range—use at() when invalid indices must be diagnosed.

phases.goal: Demonstrate interview craft: spot UB before tracing output, cite production tooling, and state pre-/post-conditions.

must_hit.point: When asked what a snippet outputs, first scan for UB, uninitialised variables, or missing virtual destructors; if UB is present, say the standard guarantees nothing rather than inventing an output.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate refuses to invent a print result under UB and names the reason.

must_hit.point: Production readiness includes compiling with -Wall -Wextra -Werror, running AddressSanitizer (-fsanitize=address) and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (-fsanitize=undefined), and using Valgrind when sanitizers are unavailable.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names compiler warning flags and at least one sanitizer or Valgrind with what it catches.

must_hit.point: Before coding, state invariants such as assuming a pointer is non-null (assert) or early-returning when a vector is empty.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate verbalises preconditions and a defensive check rather than silently assuming valid input.

probes: This function returns a pointer—how would you review it in an interview, and what tools would you mention to catch related bugs?

hints.1: Do not start by simulating output; scan ownership and lifetime first.
hints.2: If it returns a reference or pointer, trace who owns the data; then mention warnings and sanitizers.
hints.3: Flag returning a local or c_str() of a temporary as UB/dangling, state that formally nothing is guaranteed, and cite -Wall/-Wextra/-Werror plus ASan/UBSan or Valgrind.

tradeoffs.topic: Signed integer overflow vs unsigned wraparound
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Signed overflow is UB and optimisers may delete bounds checks that assume it cannot happen; unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap using modulo arithmetic.
operator[] does not check bounds to maximise performance; at() guarantees std::out_of_range on invalid access when safety matters more than the check cost.

tradeoffs.topic: Polymorphic pass-by-value vs reference or pointer
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Copying into a Base by value slices away derived members and dynamic type (e.g. print shows Base); pass Base& or Base* so virtual dispatch still reaches the derived override.

tradeoffs.topic: Escaping lambda capture by reference vs by value
tradeoffs.strong_answer: [&] on a local that dies when the function returns leaves a dangling capture; capture by value [=] or [local], and prefer returning owning objects such as std::string instead of pointers into temporaries.

tradeoffs.topic: Most vexing parse: Widget w() vs Widget w / Widget w{}
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Parentheses make the declaration parse as a function returning Widget; omit them or use uniform initialisation so you get an object (same pitfall as std::mutex m() vs std::mutex m).

gotchas.trap: Treating vector operator[] like a checked accessor and expecting a clean error on OOB.
gotchas.correction: v[i] does not bounds-check; use v.at(i) for a guaranteed std::out_of_range.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a double free fails immediately at the second delete.
gotchas.correction: Double free typically corrupts heap-manager structures and may crash much later, which makes it hard to diagnose.

gotchas.trap: Writing std::mutex m() (or Widget w()) thinking you default-constructed an object.
gotchas.correction: That declares a function; use std::mutex m; or Widget w2{}.

gotchas.trap: Mixing signed and unsigned in comparisons or downward-counting loops without warnings.
gotchas.correction: The signed value converts to unsigned (e.g. u + s with u=10 and s=-20 can make u + s > 0 true); compile with -Wsign-compare.

gotchas.trap: Comparing floats or doubles with == after decimal arithmetic.
gotchas.correction: Precision means 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is usually false; compare std::abs(a - b) against a small epsilon.

gotchas.trap: Returning temp.c_str() or capturing locals by [&] in a lambda that escapes.
gotchas.correction: The temporary or local is destroyed and the pointer/reference dangles; return by value and capture by value if the callable outlives the scope.

gotchas.trap: Calling virtual functions from a constructor or destructor expecting the most-derived override.
gotchas.correction: Only the current class's implementation runs because the derived part does not exist yet (or is already destroyed); use a separate init or pass config into the base constructor.

gotchas.trap: Depending on initialisation order of globals or statics across translation units.
gotchas.correction: Order is undefined across TUs; wrap in function-local statics (construct on first use), e.g. getDependency() returning a static.

gotchas.trap: Deleting a derived object through a non-virtual base destructor.
gotchas.correction: That is UB and typically only the base destructor runs; polymorphic bases need virtual ~Base() = default.

gotchas.trap: Using iterators after push_back or erase without updating them.
gotchas.correction: Reallocation or erase can invalidate iterators; re-assign after modification, prefer indices where appropriate, and use it = v.erase(it).

gotchas.trap: Managing a raw pointer with only a destructor and relying on the default copy constructor (Rule of 3/5).
gotchas.correction: The default copy shares the pointer, so destruction double-frees; implement destructor, copy constructor, and copy assignment (and move operations as needed).

gotchas.trap: Ordering member-initialiser-list entries differently from member declaration order.
gotchas.correction: Members initialise in declaration order regardless of list order, so y(x) can read uninitialised x; list initialisers in declaration order.
